title: Distance Teaching Experience of Campus-based Teachers at Times of Pandemic Confinement
venue: ACM 5th International Conference on Education Technology Management (ICETM 2022)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how campus-based university teachers adapted to emergency remote teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic, with a focus on student engagement, interaction, and the practical challenges of shifting traditionally in-person courses online. The authors ask how teachers adjusted their instruction, what they perceived as effective for keeping learning engaging, and whether the experience would influence future campus teaching.

The study was conducted through online semi-structured interviews with six teachers in the Department of Computer Science at Blekinge Institute of Technology in Sweden. The participants came from different computer science teaching areas, including computer security, data science, digital scheduling, software engineering, game technology, and telecommunication. The paper is not about generative AI; rather, it is about emergency distance teaching practices during the pandemic, including live lectures, recorded sessions, Zoom chats, polls, Mentimeter, Padlet, Kahoot, and related digital tools.

The authors found that interaction was harder to maintain online, especially when students kept webcams off and verbal/non-verbal cues were missing. At the same time, asynchronous tools such as chat and polls sometimes increased participation and reduced shyness barriers. Teachers valued lecture recordings for flexibility and review, but worried about reduced live interaction and procrastination. The paper concludes that teachers want better technical readiness, more use of digital tools, and a blended/flipped approach after the pandemic, while noting that remote teaching increased workload and fatigue and that VR-based solutions were seen as impractical in this context.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study with six teachers, using inductive thematic analysis. It provides contextual insight but does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility standards for causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceptions of mixed-to-positive pedagogical changes during emergency remote teaching, but no quantified intervention effect sizes or student outcome data are provided. Impact is therefore modest and unclear rather than demonstrably large.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative interview study (n=6 teachers) found that distance teaching during pandemic confinement both increased and hindered student engagement. Teachers reported improved interaction in some cases through chat, polls, and asynchronous communication, but also noted reduced verbal participation, loss of non-verbal cues, and 'Zoom fatigue' affecting engagement.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on student engagement, interactivity, and Zoom fatigue

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers perceived gains in communication, adaptability, and digital-tool use during the emergency shift to online teaching, and believed these practices could carry over into future campus-based teaching. However, the evidence is anecdotal and based on reflections from 6 Computer Science faculty members rather than direct student skill measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported reflections on adaptation, communication practices, and future pedagogical transfer

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described online recordings, quizzes, polls, and chat as useful for reaching students and enabling later review, but also emphasized increased workload from recording/editing videos, adapting assessments, ensuring legal correctness of home exams, and monitoring chat. The overall operational effect was therefore mixed: some processes became easier, while others became more time-consuming.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on workload, recording, assessment preparation, and digital tool use

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that the pandemic prompted lasting institutional changes in higher education practice, including interest in hybrid/flipped classrooms and broader adoption of digital tools in campus-based teaching. The finding is based on thematic analysis of 6 teachers and reflects perceived longer-term institutional influence rather than measured organizational outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher recommendations and perceptions about post-pandemic teaching models and institutional practice
